title: De Constantia
author: Lucius Annaeus Seneca

passages.original: Quodsi laedi nisi infirmior non potest, malus autem bono infirmior est, nec iniuria bonis nisi a dispari verenda est; iniuria in sapientem virum non cadit. Illud enim iam non es admonendus neminem bonum esse nisi sapientem. " Si iniuste," inquit, " Socrates damnatus est, iniuriam accepit."
passages.english: But if only the weaker can be harmed, and the bad man is weaker than the good, and good men need fear injury only from someone unlike them, then injury does not fall upon the wise man. For by now you do not need to be reminded that no one is good except the wise man. "If Socrates," he says, "was condemned unjustly, he received an injury."
passages.notes: Sense of the first sentence: since it is the weaker who is harmed, and harm comes only from the unlike, the wise (and good) cannot be injured. "He says" introduces an imagined objector. As transmitted, the first clause literally reads "if [one] cannot be harmed except [as] the weaker"; this is rendered by its evident sense.

passages.original: Chrysippus ait quendam indignatum, quod illum aliquis vervecem marinum dixerat. In senatu flentem vidimus Fidum Cornelium, Nasonis Ovidii generum, cum illum Corbulo struthocamelum depilatum dixisset ; adversus alia maledicta mores et vitam convulnerantia frontis illi firmitas constitit, adversus hoc tam absurdum lacrimae prociderunt ;
passages.english: Chrysippus says that a certain man was indignant because someone had called him a sea-wether. We saw Cornelius Fidus, the son-in-law of Ovidius Naso, weeping in the senate when Corbulo had called him a plucked ostrich; against other insults that wounded his character and life the firmness of his face held up, but against this one, so absurd, the tears burst out;
passages.notes: "Sea-wether" (vervex marinus, literally a castrated ram of the sea) is an obscure insult; its exact point is uncertain. "Struthocamelus" is the ostrich (literally "sparrow-camel"). The sentence continues beyond the passage.

passages.original: Ergo hoc ipsum solacio erit, etiam si nostra facilitas ultionem omiserit, futurum aliquem qui poenas exigat a procace et superbo et iniurioso, quae vitia numquam in uno homine et in una contumelia consumuntur. Respiciamus eorum exempla, quorum laudamus patientiam, ut Socratis, qui comoediarum publicatos in se et spectatos sales in partem bonam accepit risitque non minus quam cum ab uxore Xanthippe immunda aqua perfunderetur. Antistheni mater barbara et Thraessa obiciebatur ;
passages.english: So this very thing will be a comfort, even if our own easy temper has let vengeance go: that there will be someone to exact punishment from the insolent, the arrogant and the injurious man, for these vices are never used up on one person and in one insult. Let us look back at the examples of those whose patience we praise, such as Socrates, who took in good part the witticisms of the comedies, published against him and watched [by the public], and laughed no less than when he was drenched with dirty water by his wife Xanthippe. Antisthenes was taunted that his mother was a barbarian and a Thracian;
